# Decoding the Critique Mechanism in Large Reasoning Models

Hoang Phan¹ Quang H. Nguyen¹ Hung T. Q. Le¹ Xiusi Chen² Heng Ji² Khoa D.
Doan¹

¹VinUni-Illinois Smart Health Center, VinUniversity  
²University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign ^(†)^(†)thanks: Correspondence:
khoa.dd@vinuni.edu.vn.

###### Abstract

Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) exhibit backtracking and self-verification
mechanisms that enable them to revise intermediate steps and reach
correct solutions, yielding strong performance on complex logical
benchmarks. We hypothesize that such behaviors are beneficial only when
the model has sufficiently strong “critique” ability to detect its own
mistakes. This work systematically investigates how current LRMs recover
from errors by inserting arithmetic mistakes in their intermediate
reasoning steps. Notably, we discover a peculiar yet important
phenomenon: despite the error propagating throughout the entire
chain-of-thought (CoT) without any verbalized correction, the model
still reaches the correct final answer after the thinking process
finishes. This recovery implies the existence of an internal mechanism
helping the model to detect errors and trigger self-correction, which we
refer to as the hidden critique ability. Building on feature space
analysis, we identify a highly interpretable critique vector
representing this behavior. Extensive experiments across multiple model
scales and families demonstrate that steering latent representations
with this vector improves the model’s error detection capability and
enhances the performance of test-time scaling at no extra training cost.
Our findings provide a valuable understanding of LRMs’ critique
behavior, suggesting a promising direction to control and improve their
self-verification mechanism. Our code is available at:
[https://github.com/mail-research/lrm-critique-vectors](https://github.com/mail-research/lrm-critique-vectors).

## 1 Introduction

The recent wave of large reasoning models (LRMs) — including the o1
series \[[1](#bib.bib40)\], DeepSeek-R1 \[[2](#bib.bib41)\], and
Qwen3 \[[3](#bib.bib42)\] — has raised the performance ceiling on
complex, multi-step reasoning benchmarks. Recent
studies \[[2](#bib.bib41), [4](#bib.bib39)\] show that these models
exhibit human-like “aha moments”, including backtracking and
self-verification (e.g., “Wait, I made a mistake!”), resulting in
non-linear traces rather than traditional linear CoT and enabling strong
performance on complex logical benchmarks. Yet, many “aha moments” and
backtracking steps are redundant or illusory, leading to overthinking:
models produce excessive tokens, enter self-doubt loops, and often
degrade performance due to a lack of critical
thinking \[[5](#bib.bib46), [6](#bib.bib47), [7](#bib.bib4)\]. This
suggests that while models possess some “critique” ability to detect
their own mistakes, it remains intrinsically weak and not yet well
understood, underscoring the need for methods that help models to
reliably detect genuine errors, execute precise self-correction, and
eliminate decorative reasoning steps. Throughout this paper, we use the
terms critique, self-critique, and self-correction interchangeably to
refer to the ability of LRMs to detect and rectify errors.

Recent work on test-time scaling increases inference compute to enhance
reasoning performance, rather than scaling model size. For instance,
s1 \[[8](#bib.bib12)\] shows that minimal fine-tuning with budget
forcing — appending “Wait” tokens during inference — yields significant
gains, while compute-optimal strategies enable smaller models to
outperform larger ones \[[9](#bib.bib8)\]. However, test-time scaling
does not consistently improve performance \[[10](#bib.bib11),
[11](#bib.bib10)\], as its effectiveness depends on the model’s
intrinsic self-verification capacity \[[12](#bib.bib9),
[11](#bib.bib10)\]. A key bottleneck is that LLMs struggle to detect
errors in long CoTs \[[13](#bib.bib19)\], fail to self-correct without
external guidance \[[14](#bib.bib21)\], and cannot reliably identify
their own mistakes \[[15](#bib.bib22)\]. While training-based methods
improve verification capabilities \[[16](#bib.bib17), [17](#bib.bib13),
[18](#bib.bib14), [19](#bib.bib20)\], they require substantial training
costs, architectural complexity, or external tools, reducing
practicality. We hypothesize that the budget forcing approach relies
heavily on the error detection and correction ability, and investigate
whether this ability can be identified and controlled without additional
training.

![Refer to caption](2603.16331v2/main_figure.png)

Figure 1: Hidden self-correction despite erroneous reasoning in R1-32B.
Left: original correct reasoning. Right: injected error (3 + 4 = 6)
propagates to incorrect thinking conclusion (\$20), yet the model
recovers to the correct final answer (\$18). We hypothesize this
indicates implicit error detection beyond the observable CoT. Full
generation details are in
Appendix [J.1](#A10.SS1 "J.1 Full Examples of Original and Intervened Generation ‣ Appendix J Qualitative Examples ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models").

Understanding how LRMs handle errors internally requires samples where
models make mistakes and self-correct. However, we observe that such
instances are rare in standard generation. When the model answers
correctly, CoTs are typically all correct; when it is wrong, errors
persist throughout with no clear recovery. Moreover, labeling every step
is prohibitively expensive. Instead, we deliberately inject arithmetic
errors (e.g., $`3+4=6`$) at intermediate steps within the reasoning
trace and let the model continue without terminating its thinking
process
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
We then compare the thinking conclusions with the ground-truth answers
to assess recovery, yielding a scalable analysis framework without
per-step supervision. Surprisingly, we observe that despite the
corrupted reasoning from the injected errors, the model often recovers
and produces correct final answers
(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 LRMs Hiddenly Recover in the Final Answer ‣ 3 Uncovering Hidden Self-Correction ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
We call it the hidden critique ability, in which LRMs silently detect
errors inside \<think\>...\</think\> without verbalization, and rectify
them after \</think\>.

To understand this recovery, we analyze the feature space and observe a
strong separability between the error-recovery (with intervention) runs
and the standard (without intervention) runs, although both yield
correct final answers
(Section [4](#S4 "4 The Geometry of Critique Ability ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
We hypothesize that this separability captures an internal critique
mechanism, i.e., the model’s hidden ability to detect and correct errors
without explicit verbalization. This hidden capability can be
represented as a single linear direction in the activation space – which
is exactly the difference between the two mean vectors of activations of
the intervened and standard runs. We call it the critique vector and
validate its semantic meaning with logit lens analysis across model
families. To further evaluate our hypothesis and test the utility of the
critique vector, we use it to steer the LRMs and evaluate the
performance on several error-detection tasks. Experimental results show
that positive steering makes LRMs more “critical” and improves its
mistake-identification performance, while negative steering worsens it.
Finally, we show that controlling LRMs with this critique vector during
test-time scaling enables the model to detect its mistakes better and
produce more correct solutions.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

- •
  We reveal the hidden self-correction phenomenon in LRMs that, to the
  best of our knowledge, has not been documented before: injected
  arithmetic errors corrupt CoT reasoning and intermediate conclusions,
  yet the model implicitly recovers to produce the correct final
  response.
- •
  Through feature space analysis, we show that activations are highly
  separable between the error-recovery and the standard runs. Leveraging
  this separation, we extract a critique vector and rigorously validate
  its error-detection capability through logit lens analysis and
  steering experiments.
- •
  Finally, we demonstrate that the critique vector influences test-time
  scaling: amplifying it improves error recognition and final accuracy,
  while suppressing it degrades performance.

## 2 Related Work

Representation Engineering in LLMs. Representation engineering extracts
vectors from model activations to steer behavior without fine-tuning.
Early work \[[20](#bib.bib33), [21](#bib.bib32)\] computed steering
vectors from contrastive prompt pairs, enabling applications in style
control \[[22](#bib.bib31)\] and contrastive
steering \[[20](#bib.bib33)\], later extended to refusal
control \[[23](#bib.bib36), [24](#bib.bib26)\] and improved instruction
following \[[25](#bib.bib38)\]. Recent advances address polysemanticity
through feature-level steering \[[26](#bib.bib27)\] and apply these
techniques to large reasoning models (LRMs), including control over
thinking budgets \[[27](#bib.bib34)\], trace
editing \[[28](#bib.bib35)\], and reasoning
calibration \[[29](#bib.bib28)\]. Unlike prior work steering style,
length, or consistency, we uncover the hidden critique ability and
identify a critique vector that represents latent error detection,
providing mechanistic access to the internal processes behind successful
test-time scaling.

Faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning. Recent studies reveal that
reasoning traces in LRMs are often unfaithful to the model’s actual
computations — models may fail to verbalize true
reasoning \[[30](#bib.bib54), [31](#bib.bib1), [32](#bib.bib2)\],
generate misleading explanations \[[33](#bib.bib3)\], or produce
decorative “aha moments” \[[7](#bib.bib4)\]. Our work observes a related
phenomenon: models producing correct final answers despite corrupted
reasoning. However, we go beyond observation by locating this capability
in latent space, interpreting it as a critique vector, and using it to
causally control error detection and recovery.

Error Detection and Correction. Prior work reveals mixed capabilities in
LLM error detection and self-correction. While self-verification
improves reasoning \[[16](#bib.bib17)\], fundamental limitations
persist: LLMs struggle to detect errors in long CoT
traces \[[13](#bib.bib19)\], cannot reliably self-correct without
external guidance \[[14](#bib.bib21)\], and only succeed when error
locations are provided \[[15](#bib.bib22)\]. Recent approaches address
these gaps through key condition verification \[[34](#bib.bib23)\],
confidence–critique decomposition \[[35](#bib.bib24)\], or reinforcement
learning \[[36](#bib.bib25)\]. In reasoning models, self-verification
emerges as a critical ability during training \[[2](#bib.bib41)\], yet
the underlying mechanisms remain underexplored. [Lee et al.
\[37\]](#bib.bib18) examined its geometry in task-specific models, while
[Zhang et al. \[38\]](#bib.bib16) trained probes on reasoning steps
labeled by commercial models, showing that models implicitly encode
correctness information. In contrast, we extract the model’s intrinsic
critique ability without external supervision, enabling mechanistic
control over error detection across diverse logical reasoning tasks.

Test-Time Scaling. Test-time scaling shifts focus from parameter scaling
to allocating more computation during inference. Simple finetuning on
reasoning traces and appending “Wait” tokens already yield notable
gains \[[8](#bib.bib12)\], while compute-optimal strategies allow
smaller models to outperform much larger ones \[[9](#bib.bib8)\].
Follow-up work incorporates compute-optimal
allocation \[[39](#bib.bib15)\], self-verification \[[18](#bib.bib14)\],
tool-assisted verification \[[17](#bib.bib13)\], and reward models to
assess the reasoning quality \[[40](#bib.bib50), [41](#bib.bib48),
[42](#bib.bib49)\]. However, recent studies reveal limitations to this
potential, as extended thinking alone saturates and fails to scale
beyond a certain point \[[10](#bib.bib11)\]. Additionally, LRMs show
limited scaling capabilities without proper
verification \[[11](#bib.bib10)\], and scaling without verification or
RL remains suboptimal \[[12](#bib.bib9)\]. We hypothesize self-critique
to be the core mechanism underlying successful test-time scaling and
show that extracted critique vectors enable direct control over this
process.

## 3 Uncovering Hidden Self-Correction

### 3.1 Intervention Framework

LRMs typically operate in two phases: given the prompt $`q`$, they first
generate a reasoning trace $`c`$ between a special start-of-think token
$`\langle\texttt{think}\rangle`$ and an end-of-think token
$`\langle\texttt{/think}\rangle`$, and then produce the final answer
$`a`$. Formally:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
f_{\text{LRM}}:(q,\langle\texttt{think}\rangle)\mapsto(c,\langle\texttt{/think}\rangle,a).
``` |  | (1) |

Previous work has studied the model behavior under CoT interventions via
prefilling \[[43](#bib.bib7), [44](#bib.bib5)\], where a variable
content $`e`$ is integrated immediately after the thinking-start token.
This generation process can be expressed as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
f_{\text{LRM}}:(q,\langle\texttt{think}\rangle,e)\mapsto(\tilde{c},\langle\texttt{/think}\rangle,\tilde{a}).
``` |  | (2) |

Here, $`\tilde{c}`$ represents the model’s reasoning continuation after
intervention, and the complete CoT is formed by concatenating
$`e+\tilde{c}`$. The intervention $`e`$ is flexible and task-dependent;
for instance, it may be an instruction, a prompt, or another mechanism
designed to analyze specific model behaviors.

A key question in our work is whether LRMs can detect and recover from
errors during their internal reasoning. To investigate this, we inject
an arithmetic error $`e`$ (e.g., $`3+4=6`$) into the reasoning chain and
examine whether the continuation $`\tilde{c}`$ recovers from it. We
generate this error using GPT-5 with a carefully engineered prompt
$`\mathcal{P}_{\text{err}}`$ (detailed in
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 GPT-5 Instruction Prompt ‣ Appendix A System Prompt ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")):

|     |                                                           |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       f_{\texttt{GPT-5}}:(q,\mathcal{P}_{\text{err}})\mapsto e.
       ```                                                        |     | (3) |

Using this approach, we construct GSM8K-Error and MATH500-Error by
generating one error $`e`$ per question $`q`$, yielding a consistent
benchmark across all models evaluated. For evaluation, we extract the
thinking process $`\tilde{c}`$ and final answer $`a`$, then compare both
against the ground truth $`y_{q}`$ to determine whether the model can
recover from the injected errors. Unlike step-by-step supervision
methods \[[38](#bib.bib16)\] that require labeling each reasoning step,
our approach is far more efficient and scalable. Details on the error
generation process and evaluation are in
Appendix [J.1](#A10.SS1 "J.1 Full Examples of Original and Intervened Generation ‣ Appendix J Qualitative Examples ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
and
Section [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Experimental Details ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models"),
respectively.

### 3.2 LRMs Hiddenly Recover in the Final Answer

Figure 2: Distribution of reasoning-result alignment across R1 and Qwen3
model variants. The proportions represent four distinct outcomes based
on the correctness of the internal “thinking” process versus the
correctness of the final “answer” on the GSM8K-Error and MATH500-Error
benchmarks. In this paper, we analyze the self-correction mechanisms
represented by the light blue segments: ‘$`\times`$ Think $`\checkmark`$
Answer’.

We evaluate four open-source LRMs — DeepSeek-R1 (8B, 14B, 32B) and Qwen3
(4B) — on GSM8K-Error and MATH500-Error (details in Section
[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Experimental Details ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 LRMs Hiddenly Recover in the Final Answer ‣ 3 Uncovering Hidden Self-Correction ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
shows outcome distributions by the correctness of the internal reasoning
(“Thinking”) and final output (“Answer”) on the intervened datasets.

Surprisingly, beyond the dominant cases where reasoning and final
answers align (i.e., both correct or both incorrect), we observe a
significant fraction where the model’s visible reasoning $`c`$ remains
corrupted yet the final answer $`a`$ is correct. We hypothesize that in
these cases, LRMs implicitly correct the injected mistake without
verbalizing it in the CoT. We call this behavior hidden self-correction.

Specifically, on GSM8K-Error, R1 models consistently exhibit hidden
self-correction: in $`55\%--78\%`$ of cases, they produce correct final
answers while injected errors remain intact in the reasoning trace;
explicit corrections, by contrast, remain rare ($`<6\%`$). This implicit
recovery persists across model scales and extends to the more
challenging MATH500-Error ($`41\%`$–$`59\%`$).

Unlike R1 models, Qwen3-4B demonstrates powerful explicit backtracking,
recovering from injected errors in $`42.7\%`$ of GSM8K-Error cases and
$`81.9\%`$ of MATH500-Error cases. However, a moderate fraction of
samples — $`20.1\%`$ on GSM8K-Error and $`10.8\%`$ on MATH500-Error —
still show correct final answers without CoT corrections. This suggests
that the hidden self-correction mechanism exists consistently across
different model families.

Beyond our hypothesis that the model internally identifies and corrects
the injected error, two alternative explanations remain:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

To test memorization, we construct a non-public synthetic GSM8K-style
dataset and apply the same pipeline from
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Intervention Framework ‣ 3 Uncovering Hidden Self-Correction ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models");
recovery persists
(Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Does Memorization Explain the Recovery Phenomenon? ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models"),
Table [6](#A3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Results. ‣ Appendix C Does Memorization Explain the Recovery Phenomenon? ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
For the second case, we consider two settings: (1) masking the question
so the model must rely only on the corrupted CoT, and (2) requiring the
final answer to begin with “Based on my thinking above” to encourage
reliance on the trace. The $`\times`$ Think / $`\checkmark`$ Answer
pattern persists in both cases
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Analysis: Error-Injected Intervention Variants ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models"),
Figures [8](#A2.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ B.1 Qualitative Examples ‣ Appendix B Analysis: Error-Injected Intervention Variants ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")–[9](#A2.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ B.1 Qualitative Examples ‣ Appendix B Analysis: Error-Injected Intervention Variants ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models"),
Table [5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ B.2 Quantitative Results ‣ Appendix B Analysis: Error-Injected Intervention Variants ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).

Overall, these results confirm that the phenomenon reflects a hidden
self-correction mechanism, not an artifact of memorization or
trace-bypassing.

## 4 The Geometry of Critique Ability

Section [3](#S3 "3 Uncovering Hidden Self-Correction ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
shows that LRMs possess a hidden critique ability to recover from
injected errors, yet this behavior almost disappears on natural CoTs
(Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 The Geometry of Critique Ability ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
In this section, we compare these two cases to extract and analyze the
critique ability using mechanistic interpretability tools. We observe
linear separability in the latent space between the intervened
(incorrect-CoT) and baseline (correct-CoT) runs
(Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 The Linear Separability of Internal Thoughts ‣ 4 The Geometry of Critique Ability ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
This linear separability suggests that the hidden capability can be
decoded as a single direction in the activation space. We validate this
hypothesis via Logit Lens \[[45](#bib.bib45)\] and extract a steering
vector that capture the recovery mechanism.

| Cases | GSM8K |  |  |  | MATH500 |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | Q3-4B | R1-8B | R1-14B | R1-32B | Q3-4B | R1-8B | R1-14B | R1-32B |
| $`\times`$ Think, $`\times`$ Ans | $`3.9`$% | $`15.6`$% | $`6.8`$% | $`5.0`$% | $`1.5`$% | $`5.0`$% | $`4.1`$% | $`2.4`$% |
| $`\checkmark`$ Think, $`\checkmark`$ Ans | $`95.8`$% | $`81.8`$% | $`92.4`$% | $`94.0`$% | $`98.3`$% | $`95.0`$% | $`95.5`$% | $`97.4`$% |
| $`\checkmark`$ Think, $`\times`$ Ans | $`0.0`$% | $`0.7`$% | $`0.2`$% | $`0.5`$% | $`0.2`$% | $`0.0`$% | $`0.0`$% | $`0.0`$% |
| $`\times`$ Think, $`\checkmark`$ Ans | $`0.2`$% | $`1.9`$% | $`0.5`$% | $`0.5`$% | $`0.0`$% | $`0.0`$% | $`0.4`$% | $`0.2`$% |

Table 1: Distribution of reasoning and final answer correctness on GSM8K
and MATH500.

### 4.1 The Behavior on Original Samples

Section [3](#S3 "3 Uncovering Hidden Self-Correction ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
shows that LRMs secretly detect injected errors and recover in the final
answer. Here, we investigate the behavior of LRMs on original samples by
measuring the accuracy of the thinking and the final answer separately.
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 The Geometry of Critique Ability ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
demonstrates that CoT and final answer are usually consistent: when the
thinking is wrong, the model hardly fixes it and thus returns the
incorrect final answer. The recovery rate is only $`1.9\%`$ for R1-8B on
GSM8K and less than $`1\%`$ in every other case. These results suggest
that, without injected errors, LRMs do not invoke critique behavior:
correct reasoning and correct answers typically co-occur, while recovery
from faulty CoTs is rare.

### 4.2 The Linear Separability of Internal Thoughts

| Model    | GSM8K |       | MATH500 |       | Layer |
|----------|-------|-------|---------|-------|-------|
|          | AUROC | ECE   | AUROC   | ECE   |       |
| Qwen3-4B | 1.000 | 0.002 | 1.000   | 0.026 | 21    |
| R1-8B    | 0.998 | 0.019 | 0.996   | 0.022 | 31    |
| R1-14B   | 1.000 | 0.003 | 0.998   | 0.012 | 28    |
| R1-32B   | 1.000 | 0.002 | 0.997   | 0.008 | 38    |

Table 2: Linear probing results. Comparison of AUROC and ECE evaluated
on GSM8K (ID) and MATH500 (OOD) across four different models. The
reported results are selected for the best layer. Detailed results can
be found in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Additional Results of Linear Separability of Internal Thoughts ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models").

We evaluate on in-distribution (ID) GSM8K-Error and out-of-distribution
(OOD) MATH500-Error, using AUROC and Expected Calibration Error (ECE).
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 The Linear Separability of Internal Thoughts ‣ 4 The Geometry of Critique Ability ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
reports results for the best layer per model (highest ID AUROC, lowest
ID ECE), with full layer-wise results in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Additional Results of Linear Separability of Internal Thoughts ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models").

To further investigate, we compare the latent features of intervened
samples in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Uncovering Hidden Self-Correction ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
and original samples. We write $`x\sim y_{q}`$ when an output $`x`$,
which could be a reasoning conclusion $`c`$ or a final answer $`a`$,
matches the ground-truth $`y_{q}`$, and $`x\not\sim y_{q}`$ otherwise.
For 1,000 GSM8K training questions $`\mathcal{Q}_{\text{train}}`$, we
construct paired runs with identical prompts: a baseline run with
correct reasoning ($`c\sim y_{q}`$) and an intervened run with incorrect
reasoning ($`e+\tilde{c}\not\sim y_{q}`$), both of which yield correct
final answers ($`a\sim y_{q},\tilde{a}\sim y_{q}`$). As discussed above,
in the final answer the model performs hidden critique ability to
recover from mistakes. Therefore, we inspect the hidden states of the
final answers and extract the average feature vectors across answer
tokens at each layer $`\ell`$:

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle h_{\text{baseline}}^{(\ell)}(q)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|a|}\sum_{i\in a}h_{i}^{(\ell)}(q,c,a),\quad h_{\text{intervened}}^{(\ell)}(q)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\tilde{a}|}\sum_{i\in\tilde{a}}h_{i}^{(\ell)}(q,e+\tilde{c},\tilde{a}),`$ |  | (4) |

where
$`c\sim y_{q},\;a\sim y_{q},\;e+\tilde{c}\not\sim y_{q},\;\tilde{a}\sim y_{q}`$.

For each layer $`\ell`$, we train a linear probe
$`f_{\ell}(h)=W_{\ell}h+b_{\ell}`$ with
$`W_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times d}`$, where $`d`$ is the size of
feature vectors, to distinguish the baseline from intervened
activations. The probe is trained with AdamW (learning rate $`10^{-3}`$)
for 100 epochs, with a cosine schedule.

We observe consistently strong probing performance across all models and
both datasets, with near-perfect AUROC. This indicates that the
underlying activations remain linearly separable despite the matching
final answers. This separability suggests that the hidden
self-correction ability discovered in Section
[3](#S3 "3 Uncovering Hidden Self-Correction ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
corresponds to a single linear direction in the latent space.

One concern is whether this near-perfect separability reflects hidden
self-correction or an activation shift induced by the corrupted
reasoning style.
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Does the Probe Capture Critique, or Just Corrupted-Reasoning Style? ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
rules this out: recovered and unrecovered samples — despite sharing the
same corrupted CoT — remain representationally distinct.

### 4.3 Extracting the Critique Vector

Following previous works \[[21](#bib.bib32), [20](#bib.bib33)\], we
identify the critique vector as the difference-in-means between
contrastive pairs of runs constructed in
Eqn [4](#S4.E4 "Equation 4 ‣ 4.2 The Linear Separability of Internal Thoughts ‣ 4 The Geometry of Critique Ability ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models").
We consider the intervened runs in which the model performs hidden
self-correction as positive examples, and the baseline runs in which the
model merely summarizes the CoTs without invoking recovery as negative
examples.

Formally, we compute the critique vector at layer $`\ell`$ as the mean
difference between intervened and baseline activations over the training
dataset $`\mathcal{Q}_{\text{train}}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
v_{\ell}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}_{\text{train}}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{\text{train}}}\Bigl(h_{\text{intervened}}^{(\ell)}(q)-h_{\text{baseline}}^{(\ell)}(q)\Bigr).
``` |  | (5) |

### 4.4 Steering with the Critique Vector

|      |                   |       |                         |       |
|------|-------------------|-------|-------------------------|-------|
| Rank | Qwen3-4B          |       | R1-32B                  |       |
|      | Token             | Logit | Token                   | Logit |
| 1    | wrongly           | 1.78  | Wait                    | 2.68  |
| 2    | Nope              | 1.72  | 但实际上 (But actually) | 2.65  |
| 3    | 而且还 (And also) | 1.63  | 却 (But/Yet)            | 2.64  |
| 4    | really            | 1.61  | however                 | 2.60  |
| 5    | \_that            | 1.60  | but                     | 2.58  |
| 6    | Actually          | 1.60  | 不过 (However)          | 2.57  |
| 7    | 但却 (But yet)    | 1.59  | Wait                    | 2.55  |
| 8    | ?)\n\n            | 1.57  | (                       | 2.49  |

| 10   | actually          | 1.56  | However                 | 2.41  |

Table 3: Comparison of the top 10 predicted tokens and their associated
logit scores for the Qwen3-4B and R1-32B models.

We can use the critique vector in
Eqn [5](#S4.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 4.3 Extracting the Critique Vector ‣ 4 The Geometry of Critique Ability ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
to causally control and modulate the model’s hidden critique/recovery
ability. Following the standard steering approach \[[46](#bib.bib37),
[28](#bib.bib35), [24](#bib.bib26), [29](#bib.bib28),
[26](#bib.bib27)\], we add a scaled steering vector to the residual
stream immediately after the MLP layer:

|     |                                                          |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       h_{\text{steered}}^{(\ell)}=h^{(\ell)}+\alpha\,v_{\ell},
       ```                                                       |     | (6) |

where $`h^{(\ell)}`$ is the post-MLP residual stream activation at layer
$`\ell`$, $`v_{\ell}`$ is the steering vector at layer $`\ell`$, and
$`\alpha\in\mathbb{R}`$ is a scalar steering coefficient. The modified
activations $`h_{\text{steered}}^{(\ell)}`$ are then propagated through
subsequent layers, allowing the steering direction to shape the model’s
downstream generation. Intuitively, this steering vector represents the
critique ability of LRMs, which helps them detect and recover from the
injected mistakes. Positive values of $`\alpha`$ amplify the model’s
self-critique ability, whereas negative values suppress this behavior.
Further details on how we select the layer $`\ell`$ for steering are
provided in Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E How to Select the Optimal Layer for Steering? ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models").

### 4.5 Logit Lens Interpretation

In this section, we investigate the meaning of $`v_{\ell}`$ using Logit
Lens \[[45](#bib.bib45)\], which estimates the model’s belief of its
internal states. Specifically, we project $`v_{\ell}`$ into the
vocabulary space using the unembedding matrix
$`W_{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times|V|}`$, where $`|V|`$ denotes the size of
the vocabulary:

|     |                                                                 |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \text{logits}_{\ell}=v_{\ell}\,W_{U}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}.
       ```                                                              |     | (7) |

We interpret $`v_{\ell}`$ by projecting it onto the vocabulary and
extracting the highest-ranked tokens.
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.4 Steering with the Critique Vector ‣ 4 The Geometry of Critique Ability ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
lists the top 10 tokens for Qwen3-4B (layer 29) and R1-32B (layer 57).
Notably, tokens such as ‘Nope’ or ‘Wait’ rank highly — terms typically
associated with reasoning reassessment. Both models also show strong
activation of Chinese adversative markers, including

但却’ (but yet),

但实际上’ (but actually), and ‘

却’ (but/yet), suggesting that $`v_{\ell}`$ encodes critique behavior
across languages. Additional results for multiple layers can be found in
Appendix
[D](#A4 "Appendix D Additional Results of Logit Lens Interpretation ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models").

## 5 Experiments

In this section, we confirm the role of the critique vector found in
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Extracting the Critique Vector ‣ 4 The Geometry of Critique Ability ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models"),
which allows LRMs to detect errors in CoTs and correct them in the final
answer. We causally intervene on the feature space with the critique
vector to evaluate the detection ability in
Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Steering for Error Detection ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models").
Furthermore, we demonstrate the importance of the correction ability for
test-time scaling in
Section [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Test-Time Scaling with Critique Steering ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models").

### 5.1 Experimental Details

Datasets. We intervene on two widely-used mathematics benchmarks,
GSM8K \[[47](#bib.bib52)\] and MATH500 \[[48](#bib.bib53)\], to observe
model behavior under injected errors. The GSM8K training split is used
to train linear probes and derive steering vectors. For error detection
evaluation, we use two human-annotated benchmarks:
ProcessBench \[[49](#bib.bib51)\] for Olympiad-level mathematics and
BIG-Bench-Mistake \[[15](#bib.bib22)\] for diverse logical reasoning
tasks. For test-time scaling and self-correction analysis, we use our
constructed GSM8K-Error and MATH500-Error datasets alongside
BIG-Bench-Mistake, which supports correction from erroneous
chains-of-thought.

Models. We evaluate two open-source reasoning model families:
Qwen3 \[[3](#bib.bib42)\] and DeepSeek-R1 \[[2](#bib.bib41)\] across
different scales: [Qwen3-4B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-4B),
[DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B),
[DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B),
and
[DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B),
covering both Llama and Qwen architectures within R1, hereafter
Qwen3-4B, R1-8B, R1-14B, and R1-32B.

(a) ProcessBench.

(b) BIG-Bench Mistake.

Figure 3: Effect of steering coefficient $`\alpha`$ on error detection
accuracy, correct solution accuracy, and F1 score. The monotonic
relationship between $`\alpha`$ and error detection holds on both
ProcessBench and BIG-Bench Mistake. The dashed vertical line indicates
the baseline performance at $`\alpha=0`$.

Evaluation. We use
[xVerify-0.5B-I](https://huggingface.co/IAAR-Shanghai/xVerify-0.5B-I) to
verify both reasoning traces and final answers, as it provides
state-of-the-art math evaluation without requiring human annotation and
avoids template mismatch \[[50](#bib.bib43)\]. For feature analysis, we
use greedy decoding (temperature 0.0) to study deterministic internal
behavior. For steering experiments, we set the temperature to 0.6
following official guidelines to prevent reasoning loops — repetitive
thinking patterns common in reasoning models, which we also observed
with greedy decoding on challenging tasks \[[51](#bib.bib44)\]. We fix
all random seeds to 0 to ensure complete reproducibility across runs.
All experiments use two H100 GPUs.

### 5.2 Steering for Error Detection

Setup. We conduct experiments on ProcessBench and BIG-Bench Mistake,
where each sample contains a question and a CoT with at most one
erroneous step. LRMs are prompted to return the index of the incorrect
step, or $`-1`$ if no mistake exists (details in
Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Error Detection Prompt ‣ Appendix A System Prompt ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
Following the original evaluation protocol of each dataset, we report
Error Accuracy (CoTs with mistakes), Correct Accuracy (CoTs without
mistakes), and F1 Score over all samples.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 4: Qualitative example of positive steering on BIG-Bench
arithmetic task with R1-32B. There is a subtle arithmetic error
introduced in the prompt ($`7+2+20=30`$, whereas it should be $`29`$).
While the baseline model hallucinates that the math is correct during
verification, positive steering enables the model to successfully catch
the addition error.

Figure 5: Impact of steering on model accuracy for test-time scaling.
Left to right: Accuracy across three benchmarks: GSM8K-Error,
MATH500-Error, and BIG-Bench Mistake. For increasing iterations of
test-time scaling, positive steering consistently enhances the
performance of all models.

Critique vector controls the detection ability. We steer LRMs with the
critique vector using coefficients ranging from $`-1.0`$ to $`1.0`$
(Figures
[3(a)](#S5.F3.sf1 "Figure 3(a) ‣ Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 Experimental Details ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
and
[3(b)](#S5.F3.sf2 "Figure 3(b) ‣ Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 Experimental Details ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
Overall, there is a positive correlation between the steering
coefficients and model performance, confirming that the critique vector
causally controls error detection. On ProcessBench, positive steering
$`(\alpha=1.0)`$ improves error detection accuracy by $`5\%`$ on all
models. In contrast, negative steering consistently decreases it.
Similarly, on BIG-Bench Mistake, positive steering raises Qwen3-4B’s
error accuracy by 4% (from $`52\%`$ to $`56\%`$). Notably, Qwen3-4B
outperforms R1-distilled models across both datasets. A
positive-steering example is shown in
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Steering for Error Detection ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models");
corresponding negative-steering examples are deferred to
Appendix [J.2.1](#A10.SS2.SSS1 "J.2.1 Error Detection ‣ J.2 Effects of Positive and Negative Steering on LRMs ‣ Appendix J Qualitative Examples ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models").

We notice that in few scenarios, positive steering could harm the
correct accuracy, such as Qwen3-4B; qualitative examples of this failure
mode are provided in
Appendix [J.2.1](#A10.SS2.SSS1 "J.2.1 Error Detection ‣ J.2 Effects of Positive and Negative Steering on LRMs ‣ Appendix J Qualitative Examples ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models").
We hypothesize that this intervention forces the model to revise the
solution, potentially misunderstanding the correct thought and
inadvertently recognizing it as incorrect. However, the drop in correct
accuracy is insignificant, leaving the overall positive correlation
between F1 Score and steering coefficient intact.

### 5.3 Test-Time Scaling with Critique Steering

Setup. We evaluate error recovery performance on GSM8K-Error,
MATH500-Error, and BIG-Bench Mistake. For GSM8K-Error and MATH500-Error,
the model generates from the injected error until it finishes the final
answer (details of test-time scaling instruction prompt in
Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Test-time Scaling Prompt ‣ Appendix A System Prompt ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
We compare the final answer with the ground-truth label to compute the
accuracy. To test if test-time scaling helps fix injected errors, the
budget forcing \[[8](#bib.bib12)\] is applied by appending “Wait” token
at each thinking termination attempt. We report the performance at
different numbers of iterations corresponding to the number of appended
“Wait” tokens. For the critique vector effect, we perform positive
steering with a coefficient $`1.0`$ and negative steering with a
coefficient $`-1.0`$.

Critique vector steers the recovery performance.
Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.2 Steering for Error Detection ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
depicts that steering with the critique vector successfully controls the
error recovery ability. On GSM8K-Error, Qwen3-4B achieves $`77\%`$
accuracy at baseline; positive steering boosts this to nearly $`90\%`$,
while negative steering degrades the performance to slightly above
$`50\%`$. Similar trends hold across other R1-distilled models and
datasets (MATH500-Error and BIG-Bench Mistake). This confirms that error
correction is causally driven by the critique ability encoded by our
vector $`v_{\ell}`$ in
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Extracting the Critique Vector ‣ 4 The Geometry of Critique Ability ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models").

Test-time scaling corrects the injected mistake. Besides the hidden
critique ability, explicit reflection via budget forcing also recovers
from injected errors. Indeed,
Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.2 Steering for Error Detection ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
shows that appending “Wait” reliably improves the accuracy across all
models and datasets, aligning with prior findings on test-time
scaling \[[8](#bib.bib12), [9](#bib.bib8)\].

Critique vector further enhance test-time scaling. However, test-time
scaling alone does not fully repair the incorrect CoT: positive steering
consistently boosts accuracy across all forcing iterations, while
negative steering reduces it. These results indicate that hidden
critique is complementary to and can not be replaced by explicit
backtracking.

### 5.4 Steering on Standard Reasoning Benchmarks

We further apply the critique vector to original unperturbed benchmarks
(Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.4 Steering on Standard Reasoning Benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
Across all four models, positive steering yields consistent gains and
negative steering hurts across all models, confirming that the critique
direction transfers beyond the injected-error setting.

We hypothesize that there could be two reasons for the modest gains.
First, the derivation data is simple: a vector trained on GSM8K-Error
captures arithmetic-style critique and transfers weakly to AIME, where
errors reflect missing knowledge rather than failed self-checks. Second,
the steering is *unconditional*: a fixed vector is added at every step,
which on near-saturated tasks adds little signal and can over-revise
correct traces (cf.
Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Steering for Error Detection ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
Both are scalable engineering problems that we leave to future work.
More broadly, our critique vector offers a concrete representational
target for *training* better verifiers — for example, as a supervision
signal for representation-level finetuning \[[52](#bib.bib29),
[53](#bib.bib30)\] — complementing its inference-time use.

## 6 Conclusion

In this paper, we identify a *hidden critique behavior* in LRMs: they
silently recover from injected mistakes in CoTs and produce correct
final answers without verbalizing the error-detection or correction
process. Through feature analysis, we show that LRMs internally separate
intervened samples that exhibit this behavior from original ones that do
not, and we extract a *critique vector* representing this mechanism,
validated via logit lens. We identify the critique vector representing
this hidden mechanism and validate it through logit lens analysis.
Empirically, steering with this vector successfully controls error
detection across several benchmarks and models. We also show that
test-time scaling relies on critique ability and can be combined with
critique steering to further enhance correction performance. Our
findings shed light on the role of critique ability in current LRMs and
open many interesting questions. Future work should investigate whether
this behavior stems from pre- or post-training and how it emerges. Since
hidden critique ability leads LRMs to silently correct errors without
verbalizing them in CoTs, its impact on CoT faithfulness, alignment, and
other properties warrants further study. Finally, leveraging this
ability to improve test-time scaling methods such as verifier-based
approaches, self-consistency, and self-correction prompting remains an
exciting direction we leave to future work.

## Appendix A System Prompt

### A.1 GPT-5 Instruction Prompt

The following system prompt $`\mathcal{P}_{\text{err}}`$ was used to
generate incorrect reasoning steps:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### A.2 Error Detection Prompt

We evaluate reasoning error detection using two benchmarks: ProcessBench
and BIG-Bench-Mistake, each with its own prompting format.

For ProcessBench, we follow the original critique-based prompting scheme
exactly as implemented in the official repository.¹¹ 1
[https://github.com/QwenLM/ProcessBench](https://github.com/QwenLM/ProcessBench)
The model is provided with a math problem and a paragraph-structured
solution trace, and is instructed to identify the earliest paragraph
containing an error, or return $`-1`$ if no error is present.

For BIG-Bench-Mistake, we follow the original task-specific templates
provided by the authors.²² 2
[https://github.com/WHGTyen/BIG-Bench-Mistake](https://github.com/WHGTyen/BIG-Bench-Mistake)
We observe that strong reasoning models often solve the problem directly
rather than performing error detection. To maintain the original task
structure while enforcing focused evaluation, we prepend a minimal
instruction requiring the model to identify incorrect steps only.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### A.3 Test-time Scaling Prompt

We perform test-time scaling by injecting a corrupted chain-of-thought
(CoT) into the model’s intermediate thinking process and allowing the
model to continue generating. This setup simulates partial erroneous
reasoning and evaluates whether extended inference can recover from the
injected mistake.

Concretely, each generation follows the structure:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

After the model completes its reasoning, we optionally append the token
“Wait” multiple times to extend inference depth. This simple control
mechanism encourages backtracking and revision of earlier steps,
following prior work (e.g., \[[8](#bib.bib12), [11](#bib.bib10),
[10](#bib.bib11)\]).

## Appendix B Analysis: Error-Injected Intervention Variants

In
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Intervention Framework ‣ 3 Uncovering Hidden Self-Correction ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
and
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models"),
we report the phenomenon in which LRMs often produce a correct final
answer despite a corrupted CoT caused by injected errors ($`\times`$
Think, $`\checkmark`$ Answer). To probe how robust this phenomenon is,
we design several *error-injected variants* of the base intervention.
The injected error is identical across all variants; only the
surrounding context changes:

- •
  (a) Wait-once
  (Figure [6](#A2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ B.1 Qualitative Examples ‣ Appendix B Analysis: Error-Injected Intervention Variants ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
  A single *“Wait”* token is appended after the injected error,
  mimicking the test-time scaling cue of [Muennighoff et al.
  \[8\]](#bib.bib12). This variant tests whether forcing the model to
  backtrack enables it to self-correct its reasoning.
- •
  (b) Misprint
  (Figure [7](#A2.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ B.1 Qualitative Examples ‣ Appendix B Analysis: Error-Injected Intervention Variants ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
  We close ⟨/think⟩ immediately after the injected error, with no
  continued reasoning. This variant tests whether the model can recover
  from the injected error alone, before it corrupts the entire reasoning
  trace.
- •
  (c) Question-masked
  (Figure [8](#A2.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ B.1 Qualitative Examples ‣ Appendix B Analysis: Error-Injected Intervention Variants ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
  The prompt is masked, so the model generates the final answer using
  only the corrupted CoT as context. This setting tests if the model
  actually recovers from the error or simply ignores the CoT.
- •
  (d) Answer-prefix
  (Figure [9](#A2.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ B.1 Qualitative Examples ‣ Appendix B Analysis: Error-Injected Intervention Variants ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
  The final-answer segment is forced to begin with *“Based on my
  thinking above,”*. This instruction-prompting variant explicitly
  encourages the model to revisit and rely on the reasoning trace.

### B.2 Quantitative Results

Table [5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ B.2 Quantitative Results ‣ Appendix B Analysis: Error-Injected Intervention Variants ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
compares each variant against the *intervened-local* baseline from
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 LRMs Hiddenly Recover in the Final Answer ‣ 3 Uncovering Hidden Self-Correction ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models"),
and the recovery phenomenon persists in every setting. Under
*Wait-once*, the rate falls on GSM8K because the explicit cue lets the
model fix the error in plain text, but rises slightly on MATH-500, in
line with overthinking on harder problems \[[5](#bib.bib46)\].
*Misprint* attains the highest recovery rate, suggesting that even
without error propagation through the rest of the CoT, the model
self-corrects even more strongly. Surprisingly, under *Question-masked*,
the model still recovers at a rate close to the baseline despite having
only the corrupted CoT as context. *Answer-prefix* also lowers the rate
slightly, but the phenomenon clearly persists for the larger models
(R1-14B and R1-32B).

### B.3 Does the Model Simply Ignore the Wrong CoT?

An alternative explanation for the
$`\times`$ Think / $`\checkmark`$ Final phenomenon is that the model
simply discards the corrupted trace and re-solves the problem when
generating the final answer:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The *Question-masked* and *Answer-prefix* variants are designed to test
this hypothesis by forcing greater reliance on the corrupted trace. In
*Question-masked*, the question is removed, leaving the corrupted CoT as
the only available context. In *Answer-prefix*, the final answer is
explicitly prompted to refer back to the reasoning trace. In both cases,
the $`\times`$ Think / $`\checkmark`$ Answer phenomenon persists,
especially for larger models.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Appendix C Does Memorization Explain the Recovery Phenomenon?

A key concern with the observation in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Uncovering Hidden Self-Correction ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
is that the distilled model may have been trained on public benchmarks
such as GSM8K. If so, the model might have memorized the final answers
to these examples and could recover them without relying on the
information contained in the corrupted reasoning trace. To rule out this
possibility, we construct synthetic examples that do not appear in
training and rerun the protocol from
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Intervention Framework ‣ 3 Uncovering Hidden Self-Correction ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
on them:

-  Step 1.
  For each GSM8K-test problem, we prompt GPT-5 to modify the numbers,
  names, and surface context while preserving the original step-by-step
  solution structure, yielding a new question with a single, consistent
  ground-truth answer.
-  Step 2.
  We retain only rewrites whose problem statement and answer are
  logically consistent.
-  Step 3.
  We apply the *intervened-local* corruption protocol from
  Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Intervention Framework ‣ 3 Uncovering Hidden Self-Correction ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
  to the synthetic dataset and measure the same
  $`\times`$ Think / $`\checkmark`$ Final recovery rate.

The exact prompt template used in Step 1 is given below; we instantiate
it once per GSM8K problem and query GPT-5 with structured JSON output.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

An example of a synthetic sample:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

##### Results.

Table [6](#A3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Results. ‣ Appendix C Does Memorization Explain the Recovery Phenomenon? ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
reports the recovery rate on the synthetic dataset alongside the
original GSM8K-test numbers. Recovery rates remain large on the
synthetic side – $`48.72\%`$ for Qwen3-4B and above $`68\%`$ for all
three R1 variants – and stay close to the original GSM8K rates for the
larger R1 models. Since the question, context, and final answer have all
been altered and cannot have appeared in training or distillation data,
this rules out memorization of the original answer as the explanation
for the phenomenon.

| Model    | Original GSM8K-test | Synthetic GSM8K-test |
|----------|---------------------|----------------------|
| Qwen3-4B | 20.12               | 48.72                |
| R1-8B    | 55.12               | 68.54                |
| R1-14B   | 77.43               | 71.23                |
| R1-32B   | 74.00               | 71.58                |

the original and synthetic intervention on GSM8K-test.

To validate the robustness of the identified steering vectors
$`v_{\ell}`$, we analyze the trajectory of the top projected tokens with
Logit Lens across five consecutive layers. Tables
[7](#A4.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix D Additional Results of Logit Lens Interpretation ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
and
[8](#A4.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix D Additional Results of Logit Lens Interpretation ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
present the evolution of the top 10 tokens and their associated logit
scores for Qwen3-4B (Layers 29–33) and R1-32B (Layers 55–58),
respectively. Comparing the two models reveals some qualitative
differences in their self-critique mechanisms. While R1-32B (Table
[8](#A4.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix D Additional Results of Logit Lens Interpretation ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models"))
tends toward the interruptive tokens such as ‘Wait’ or ‘

但实际上’ (but actually), Qwen3-4B (Table
[7](#A4.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix D Additional Results of Logit Lens Interpretation ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models"))
exhibits a preference for direct negation and correction tokens, such as
‘wrongly’, ‘Nope’, and ‘Actually’ throughout Layers 29–33. We
hypothesize that this distinction may suggest that the extracted vector
in Qwen3-4B encodes a more immediate “fact-checking” signal, whereas the
vector in R1-32B captures a specialized backtracking behavior. This may
also explain the significant difference in proportions of ‘$`\times`$
Think $`\checkmark`$ Answer’ and ‘$`\checkmark`$ Think $`\checkmark`$
Answer’ in Figure
[2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 LRMs Hiddenly Recover in the Final Answer ‣ 3 Uncovering Hidden Self-Correction ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
between the two models.

## Appendix E How to Select the Optimal Layer for Steering?

Following previous works \[[7](#bib.bib4), [29](#bib.bib28),
[46](#bib.bib37), [28](#bib.bib35)\], we only apply the steering vector
to the LRM for one selected layer. In this section, we describe the
procedure for identifying the optimal layer that is the most
representative of the self-critique mechanism. Consistent with [Sun et
al. \[28\]](#bib.bib35), for each LRM, we apply the steering vector as
defined in Eq.
[6](#S4.E6 "Equation 6 ‣ 4.4 Steering with the Critique Vector ‣ 4 The Geometry of Critique Ability ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
to each layer independently using scaling factors
$`\alpha\in\{-1.0,1.0\}`$. All experiments for layer-wise steering are
conducted on the GSM8K training split (Figure
[10](#A5.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ Appendix E How to Select the Optimal Layer for Steering? ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
We define the optimal layer as the one which yields the greatest
accuracy differential between positive (1.0) steering and negative
(-1.0) steering. At this layer, the effect of self-correction
enhancement or suppression is the most pronounced, suggesting that this
layer acts as the primary locus for the model’s internal self-critique
processes. As demonstrated in Table
[9](#A5.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix E How to Select the Optimal Layer for Steering? ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
and Figure
[10](#A5.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ Appendix E How to Select the Optimal Layer for Steering? ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models"),
the differential between positive and negative steering ($`\Delta`$) is
the most prominent for middle layers, with $`\Delta`$ even exceeding
$`38\%`$ for Layer 21 of Qwen3-4B.

Figure 10: Layer-wise steering results. The separation between the
performance of positive and negative steering is minimal for early and
late layers. For middle layers, this performance gap is the most
noticeable.

| Model    | $`\alpha=0.0`$ | $`\alpha=-1.0`$ | $`\alpha=1.0`$ | $`\Delta`$ | Layer |
|----------|----------------|-----------------|----------------|------------|-------|
| Qwen3-4B | 42.36          | 25.00           | 63.72          | 38.72      | 21    |
| R1-8B    | 57.03          | 53.36           | 73.48          | 20.13      | 13    |
| R1-14B   | 80.99          | 73.71           | 85.64          | 11.93      | 28    |
| R1-32B   | 79.42          | 69.74           | 86.25          | 16.51      | 44    |

Table 9: Results of the optimal layer. Overall accuracy (%) of the
optimal layer evaluated on the training split of GSM8K for baseline
($`\alpha=0.0`$), positive steering ($`\alpha=1.0`$), negative steering
($`\alpha=-1.0`$), and the difference between positive and negative
steering ($`\Delta`$).

## Appendix F Additional Results of Linear Separability of Internal Thoughts

In Section
[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 The Linear Separability of Internal Thoughts ‣ 4 The Geometry of Critique Ability ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models"),
we have provided the results of the best layer for the linear probing
experiments. In this section, we outline the results (AUROC and ECE) for
all layers across four LRMs: Qwen3-4B, R1-8B, R1-14B, and R1-32B.

As shown in the AUROC plots of Figure
[11](#A6.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ Appendix F Additional Results of Linear Separability of Internal Thoughts ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
(left column), linear separability saturates near 1.0 for the majority
of the network depth across all models. The GSM8K dataset
(in-distribution, orange) consistently exhibits high and stable
separability almost immediately from the initial layers. In addition, we
observe that lower layers tend to be poorly calibrated (high ECE), with
calibration improving significantly in the middle layers. Comparing the
two datasets, GSM8K demonstrates consistently lower Expected Calibration
Error and smoother layer-wise progression compared to MATH500. The
MATH500 dataset exhibits considerably higher variance and erratic spikes
in ECE. However, for most layers, the performance of the linear prober
for GSM8K and MATH500 remains close, suggesting this separability has a
high level of generalization.

Figure 11: Layer-wise linear probing results. Left to right: AUROC and
ECE for GSM8K (in-distribution) and MATH500 (out-of-distribution). For
both settings, the linear prober can achieve near-perfect AUROC and low
ECE at several layers.

## Appendix G Does the Probe Capture Critique, or Just Corrupted-Reasoning Style?

In
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 The Linear Separability of Internal Thoughts ‣ 4 The Geometry of Critique Ability ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models"),
we trained a linear probe on baseline (unintervened, correct CoT) versus
intervened-and-recovered (corrupted CoT) activations and observed
near-perfect separability. A natural question follows:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

We address this concern with two analyses:

1.  1.
    Project intervened-and-unrecovered samples onto the pretrained probe
    (Section [G.1](#A7.SS1 "G.1 Project intervened-and-unrecovered samples onto the pretrained probe ‣ Appendix G Does the Probe Capture Critique, or Just Corrupted-Reasoning Style? ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).

    - •
      What we do: Similar to
      Eq. [4](#S4.E4 "Equation 4 ‣ 4.2 The Linear Separability of Internal Thoughts ‣ 4 The Geometry of Critique Ability ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models"),
      we extract the average activations of final-answer tokens from
      intervened samples that remain unrecovered ($`\times`$ Think,
      $`\times`$ Ans), and project them using the pretrained probe from
      Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 The Linear Separability of Internal Thoughts ‣ 4 The Geometry of Critique Ability ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models").
    - •
      Expected result: A high recovered-class rate would suggest that
      the probe mainly captures general CoT corruption style, which is
      shared across both groups. In contrast, a low rate would suggest
      that the probe reflects a hidden critique ability that
      distinguishes successful recovery from incorrect reasoning.
2.  2.
    Train a new probe on equally corrupted trajectories
    (Section [G.2](#A7.SS2 "G.2 Train a new probe on equally corrupted trajectories ‣ Appendix G Does the Probe Capture Critique, or Just Corrupted-Reasoning Style? ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).

    - •
      What we do: We train a new probe from scratch using activations
      from recovered and unrecovered samples, both of which contain the
      same injected error style.
    - •
      Expected result: If these activations are separable, this would
      suggest that the model contains an internal mechanism that
      distinguishes successful recovery from failure, rather than a
      difference caused merely by the corrupted CoT style.

### G.1 Project intervened-and-unrecovered samples onto the pretrained probe

Setup. We freeze the pretrained probe from
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 The Linear Separability of Internal Thoughts ‣ 4 The Geometry of Critique Ability ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
and evaluate it on held-out GSM8K-test trajectories. These trajectories
are split into *recovered* ($`\times`$ Think, $`\checkmark`$ Ans) and
*unrecovered* ($`\times`$ Think, $`\times`$ Ans), and their activations
are projected onto the probe. We additionally evaluate two corruption
variants unseen during probe training, *Question-masked*
(Figure [8](#A2.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ B.1 Qualitative Examples ‣ Appendix B Analysis: Error-Injected Intervention Variants ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models"))
and *Misprint*
(Figure [7](#A2.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ B.1 Qualitative Examples ‣ Appendix B Analysis: Error-Injected Intervention Variants ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")),
as defined in
Section [B](#A2 "Appendix B Analysis: Error-Injected Intervention Variants ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models").
For each population, we report the rate classified as *recovered* (the
positive class).

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Model | Original |  | Question masking |  | Misprinting |  |
|  | Unrecovered | Recovered | Unrecovered | Recovered | Unrecovered | Recovered |
| Qwen3-4B | 64.22 | 99.53 | 67.58 | 99.38 | 65.27 | 100.00 |
| R1-8B | 67.38 | 99.78 | 66.00 | 99.45 | 69.96 | 99.61 |
| R1-14B | 68.49 | 98.65 | 45.97 | 99.76 | 68.64 | 100.00 |
| R1-32B | 67.82 | 99.75 | 33.71 | 99.88 | 67.82 | 99.80 |

Table 10: Rate (%) of held-out activations classified as *recovered* by
the base probe of
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 The Linear Separability of Internal Thoughts ‣ 4 The Geometry of Critique Ability ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models").
A random classifier scores around $`50\%`$.

Results. Recovered trajectories are classified as positive at very high
rates, reaching at least $`98.6\%`$ across all models and unseen
variants. In contrast, unrecovered samples score only between
$`33.71\%`$ and $`69.96\%`$, close to the $`50\%`$ binary baseline,
despite sharing the same corrupted CoT style. This indicates that the
pretrained probe does not merely detect corrupted reasoning. Rather, it
decodes a positive signal only when the model successfully recovers,
supporting the interpretation that the probe captures a hidden critique
ability.

### G.2 Train a new probe on equally corrupted trajectories

Setup. We train a fresh logistic-regression probe to distinguish
*recovered* intervened trajectories ($`\times`$ Think, $`\checkmark`$
Ans) from *unrecovered* intervened trajectories ($`\times`$ Think,
$`\times`$ Ans). Both classes contain the same injected-error style, so
the probe cannot rely on whether the CoT is corrupted. Instead, any
separability must come from differences associated with the recovery
outcome. The probe is trained on GSM8K-train activations using
class-balanced cross-entropy, since the two classes are not equally
represented. For each model, we train at the steering layer used
throughout the paper, selected by the procedure in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E How to Select the Optimal Layer for Steering? ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models").
We evaluate the resulting probe on GSM8K-test as the in-distribution
(ID) setting, and on MATH500-test as the out-of-distribution (OOD)
setting.

|          |       |        |        |         |        |
|----------|-------|--------|--------|---------|--------|
| Model    | Layer | GSM8K  |        | MATH500 |        |
|          |       | AUROC  | ECE    | AUROC   | ECE    |
| Qwen3-4B | 21    | 0.9911 | 0.0262 | 0.9557  | 0.1154 |
| R1-8B    | 13    | 0.9146 | 0.0676 | 0.8560  | 0.0580 |
| R1-14B   | 28    | 0.8856 | 0.0732 | 0.8776  | 0.2532 |
| R1-32B   | 44    | 0.9122 | 0.0771 | 0.8801  | 0.2524 |

Table 11: Linear separability of *recovered* vs. *unrecovered*
intervened trajectories.

Results. The recovered/unrecovered probe achieves strong separability
across all models, with AUROC above $`0.88`$ on GSM8K-test and above
$`0.85`$ on MATH500-test. Calibration is very good on GSM8K-test, with
ECE below $`0.08`$ for all models. On MATH500-test, ECE remains low for
Qwen3-4B and R1-8B, but is higher for R1-14B and R1-32B; nevertheless,
AUROC remains strong. Since both classes share the same corrupted CoT
style, this activation separability cannot be explained by injected
errors alone. Instead, it suggests that when the model successfully
recovers from wrong reasoning, its representations shift in a distinct
way, which we later interpret as a decoded critique ability.

## Appendix H Comparison with Token Embedding Baseline

A simple comparison for the critic vector from
Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Steering for Error Detection ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
is to steer instead with the input embedding of an error-related token.
We use the token wrong – the most direct lexical proxy for an error
signal – and take its input embedding
$`e_{\mathrm{wrong}}=\mathrm{embed}(\mathrm{tok}(\text{``wrong''}))`$ as
a steering vector.

Setup. We inject $`e_{\mathrm{wrong}}`$ at the same steering layer used
for the critic vector – layer $`21`$ for Qwen3-4B, $`13`$ for R1-8B,
$`28`$ for R1-14B, and $`44`$ for R1-32B, selected by the procedure in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E How to Select the Optimal Layer for Steering? ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
– with scaling factor $`\alpha\in\{-1,+1\}`$, and follow the protocol of
Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Steering for Error Detection ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models").
We evaluate both vectors on ProcessBench \[[49](#bib.bib51)\] and
BIG-Bench Mistake \[[15](#bib.bib22)\], reporting Accuracy and F1.

Results.
Tables [12](#A8.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Appendix H Comparison with Token Embedding Baseline ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
and [13](#A8.T13 "Table 13 ‣ Appendix H Comparison with Token Embedding Baseline ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
report each steering vector as a delta relative to the unsteered
baseline. The critic vector behaves as a clean axis: at $`\alpha{=}-1`$
Accuracy and F1 drop on every model on both benchmarks, and at
$`\alpha{=}+1`$ they rise on every model on both benchmarks. The
wrong-embedding shows no such trend: its deltas are small and
inconsistent in sign across models and benchmarks, so flipping its scale
does not flip behavior the way a steering direction should. This
indicates that the critic vector is non-trivial to find: it is not
recovered by simply taking the input embedding of an error-related
token.

## Appendix I OOD Generalization of the Critic Vector

Throughout the main paper, the critic vector derived from GSM8K already
demonstrates the controllability of critique behavior. Here we further
test whether the same effect generalizes to a different source of
training data.

Setup. For each model, we recompute the critic vector from the MATH-500
training split following the exact procedure of
Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Steering for Error Detection ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models"),
and inject it at the same per-model steering layer
(Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E How to Select the Optimal Layer for Steering? ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")).
We then sweep $`\alpha\in\{-1.0,-0.8,\ldots,+1.0\}`$ and measure
Accuracy and F1 on the Omnimath and OlympiadBench splits of
ProcessBench, averaged. Both splits come from problem sources that are
distinct from GSM8K and MATH-500, making them a clean OOD test and
sufficient evidence that the vectors generalize beyond their source
data.

Results.
Tables [14](#A9.T14 "Table 14 ‣ Appendix I OOD Generalization of the Critic Vector ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
and [15](#A9.T15 "Table 15 ‣ Appendix I OOD Generalization of the Critic Vector ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
show a consistent positive correlation between $`\alpha`$ and
error-detection ability for both sources: $`\alpha{>}0`$ improves
Accuracy and F1 on every model, and $`\alpha{<}0`$ degrades them. The
MATH-500-sourced vector exerts a notably stronger pull on the larger
models, with much sharper degradation under negative steering (e.g.,
$`-16.15`$ Acc / $`-21.75`$ F1 on R1-14B and $`-20.15`$ Acc / $`-26.85`$
F1 on R1-32B at $`\alpha{=}-1.0`$) and larger gains under positive
steering (e.g., $`+5.20`$ Acc on R1-32B at $`\alpha{=}+0.4`$, $`+5.00`$
Acc / $`+4.98`$ F1 on R1-14B at $`\alpha{=}+0.8`$). This is consistent
with the observation that steering vectors generalize better when
derived from harder data \[[54](#bib.bib6)\], and points to a promising
direction: scaling the source data used to extract critique behavior. A
thorough study of this scaling is beyond the scope of this work.

### J.2 Effects of Positive and Negative Steering on LRMs

In this section, we present a qualitative analysis of R1-32B model’s
reasoning behaviors under the influence of steering vectors derived from
the critique mechanism. We examine three distinct configurations: the
Baseline Model (Coefficient 0.0), Positive Steering (Coefficient +1.0),
and Negative Steering (Coefficient -1.0). The examples, selected from
GSM8K samples of ProcessBench and GSM8K-Error, illustrate how steering
modulates the model’s capacity for error detection, semantic
interpretation, and arithmetic verification. For this section, ellipsis
is used with “…” to truncate model responses for brevity and clarity.

#### J.2.1 Error Detection

We first examine how steering affects error detection capability,
drawing on examples from ProcessBench-GSM8K and GSM8K-Error. These cases
reveal two complementary failure modes that positive and negative
steering address in opposite directions: missing genuine errors and
hallucinating errors in correct solutions.

As shown in
Figures [13](#A10.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ J.2.1 Error Detection ‣ J.2 Effects of Positive and Negative Steering on LRMs ‣ Appendix J Qualitative Examples ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
and [14](#A10.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ J.2.1 Error Detection ‣ J.2 Effects of Positive and Negative Steering on LRMs ‣ Appendix J Qualitative Examples ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models"),
positive steering enhances the model’s ability to detect subtle
reasoning errors while avoiding false positives. In contrast,
Figure [15](#A10.F15 "Figure 15 ‣ J.2.1 Error Detection ‣ J.2 Effects of Positive and Negative Steering on LRMs ‣ Appendix J Qualitative Examples ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
demonstrates that negative steering suppresses critical verification,
causing the model to accept erroneous premises without scrutiny.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 13: Qualitative example of positive steering on a GSM8K question
from ProcessBench with R1-32B model. The proposed solution makes an
unjustified assumption about the work schedule (5 days vs 7 days). The
Baseline model accepts this assumption as “standard”, while the steered
model critically analyzes the specific phrasing “entire week” and
identifies the discrepancy.

baseline model hallucinates a logic error, incorrectly arguing that the
total budget (\$48) should be used for the counterfactual, ignoring that
the CD was still purchased. The positive steering helps the model
successfully verify the correct logic: money saved equals the cost of
the unpurchased item (\$44).

Figure 15: Qualitative example of negative steering on
ProcessBench-GSM8K with R1-32B model. The prompt contains a logical

negative steering suppresses this critical check and accepts the
erroneous premise.

#### J.2.2 Test-Time Scaling

We next examine how steering interacts with the model’s internal
self-verification behavior with test-time scaling methods.

Figures [16](#A10.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ J.2.2 Test-Time Scaling ‣ J.2 Effects of Positive and Negative Steering on LRMs ‣ Appendix J Qualitative Examples ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
and [17](#A10.F17 "Figure 17 ‣ J.2.2 Test-Time Scaling ‣ J.2 Effects of Positive and Negative Steering on LRMs ‣ Appendix J Qualitative Examples ‣ Decoding the Critique Mechanism inLarge Reasoning Models")
illustrate that positive steering enables successful error recovery
during the “Wait” phase, whereas negative steering causes the model to
rationalize and reinforce injected errors rather than correct them.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 16: Qualitative example of positive steering on GSM8K-Error with
R1-32B model. The baseline model uses a multiplication error
($`5\times 8=30`$) and confirms it during self-verification
($`70+30=100`$). Positive steering initially makes the same error but
successfully catches it during the “Wait” phase, correcting the
allowance to $`40`$ and the final answer to $`60`$.

ProcessBench-GSM8K with R1-32B model. The prompt context introduces an
arithmetic error (\$3+\$2=\$6 instead of \$5). The baseline model
initially adopts the error but triggers a self-correction after
generating “Wait,” re-evaluating the costs. The negatively steered model
````
